title: From Florida to New Hampshire: Why one student chose UNH to study marine biology - University of New Hampshire
content: Meet Emma Rawlson, a junior marine, estuarine, and freshwater biology major at the University of New Hampshire. Emma shares how her passion for marine animals has led to hands-on research opportunities. She also reflects on the value of undergraduate research and how her experiences at UNH are preparing her for a career in marine biology and conservation. I chose UNH mainly because it has an exceptional program for my major, which is research-driven given the school’s R1 research status. Additionally, UNH has a beautiful campus full of nature and critters. It's also in a great location that is close to Boston and many beaches. You can find the taxidermy of one of UNH’s original mascots, Maizie, in the UNH Archives on the bottom floor of the library. Don’t be afraid to be ambitious and go after your goals. Your college experience is really dependent on what you make of it. Also, maintain an open mind when it comes to opportunities or involvement. You never know where something might lead you. My favorite course I’ve taken thus far at UNH was Marine Mammal Biology and Conservation with Michelle Fournet. I gained a thorough understanding of various aspects of marine mammal social dynamics, anatomy, history, and more. My brain is now filled with endless marine mammal fun facts. Since I was seven years old, I knew I wanted to work with marine animals. I am absolutely fascinated with the underwater world and the marvelous creatures and mysteries within the ocean. I have always had a passion for marine animals and a drive to protect and advocate for them. Therefore, there was no question in my mind when I chose to be a MEFB major. After graduation, I plan to pursue a master's degree and a career in marine biology, focusing on field research and conservation. Through hands-on experiences in classes and work in a research lab, I have developed an extensive skill set that is vital for an aspiring scientist. As someone who seeks to enter the field of research, having the opportunity to conduct research during my undergrad will significantly help me after graduation. I work as a research assistant for the New Hampshire Lakes Lay Monitoring Program (LLMP). Throughout my sophomore year, I spent a significant amount of time analyzing water samples from Nippo Lake in Barrington, NH. I spent time counting and identifying plankton species in the samples. Additionally, I examined trophic conditions, water quality, and the health of the lake's aquatic food web. I presented my research at the COLSA Undergraduate Research Conference. title: Shannon Garvey: A UNH success story - The New Hampshire
content: In May of 2026, UNH English MFA (Master of Fine Arts) graduate Shannon Garvey received her first major publication with her novel, June Baby. Published and distributed by Random House and Thousand Voices Books, June Baby was a USA Today National Bestseller upon release, garnering acclaim from readers and critics alike. Bestselling author Coco Mellers describes the story as a “work of growing up” that is both “tender and precise,” with “Garvey’s prose [revealing] a writer of real emotional intelligence and depth.” The New York Times Book Review called the story an “old-fashioned love letter to summer romance, sun-fueled creativity and long rides on rusty bikes” — an “outsider’s story [that] unfolds in the voice of an insider.” Throughout our conversation, Garvey touched on what it has felt like to be propelled into literary success. In regards to the book tour she embarked on over the summer, she emphasized how “amazing [it was] to see [June Baby] connect with readers.” She goes on to say, “I spent four years writing it...I’m sure I would be nervous if I was talking about anything else in the world, but this is the one thing that I know best.” June Baby opens with seventeen year-old Ruth who, after losing her mother to cancer, leaves to live on a wealthy remote island with renowned photographer Diana Beckett. Ten years later, after tragedy upends her life again, Ruth must embark on a journey of mystery and self-discovery to reexamine everything she thought she knew about her past. It’s a coming-of-age story that explores both love and grief, embracing the duality between loss and possibility in one’s life. Describing her process, Garvey says that “writing a novel is such an experience, in empathy and curiosity; every day, curious to see where the story is going to lead and exercising this really beautiful empathy for characters that might not exist, but you are, every second, wondering how it might feel to be them in this scenario.” Garvey then discusses her emotional and physical attachment to a specific place, and how that manifested through her characters. “With Ruth, I was really interested in writing about somebody who was in love with a place, so the book is set on Block Island, a very small island off of Rhode Island,” the state in which Garvey herself grew up. She states she has been “fascinated by Block Island since [she] was a child,” and, through her writing, has been enamoured with the question of “what somebody might do to hold onto a place that they love that much.” Garvey makes it clear that Ruth is not her, but some of Ruth’s “fears and thoughts about the world” are things Garvey has thought and felt at various points in her life. “These characters aren't people you know at all, but to write them, you are drawing on that reservoir of your own emotions and your own connections to others.” As impressive as her novel’s acclaim is for an author and their debut work, Garvey is not the only one ecstatic about her recent success. In fact, she began writing June Baby while studying in UNH’s English MFA program, where the book eventually flourished into her thesis. She details the process. “The MFA thesis has to be 150 pages, and it can either be a collection of short stories or a novel excerpt,” but the workshop-based program “is really built around short stories...I knew from the beginning that I wanted my thesis to be a novel because I wanted to have the opportunity to have incredible writers like Tom [Payne] and Ann Williams and Jaed Coffin have their eyes on it…I thought that would be really valuable.” Of her time in the MFA program, she says “that there’s something really special about being one around a group of people who are taking the same thing you are very seriously…there’s something really transformational about inhaling that much work.” According to writer, professor, and head of the MFA department Thomas Payne, “the MFA program in Creative Writing has graduated any number of stellar writers of poetry, fiction and memoir over our last 50 years as a nationally-known program. But for Shannon to rocket out of UNH onto the Today show with basically her MFA thesis (this novel) a couple of years after graduating? That's just jaw dropping.” Garvey graduated in 2017 with a B.A. in Neuroscience and Behavior, and while in the MFA program, she taught undergraduate classes. These formative years provided her with an ever-deepening understanding of writing, literature, and what it means to find yourself through a work of art. Payne describes the “feeling” he had that Garvey was “going to hit a home run” after years of “knowing her fiction [and] seeing drafts of [June Baby].” In addition to June Baby’s popularity, Garvey has made a name for herself through her shorter works in the Saturday Evening Post and her feature on the Peabody-Award winning Moth Radio Hour. Now, after being on the “Today” show—which she considers to have been “incredibly surreal”—and in a variety of national magazines from Vogue to People, Garvey is well-underway on her second novel. “My way of dealing with the unknowns of this industry is always to be grateful for what has come to pass, and do the work every day…then, you know, we’ll see what happens.” Catch Shannon Garvey’s reading and Q&A for UNH’s Writer Series on Thursday, Oct. 22 at 5pm in Hamilton Smith Hall. The event was organized by Thomas Payne and the MFA department, and he hopes that “any UNH undergrad who wants to be a writer” comes to the event.

title: Shaheen and DiLorenzo share thoughts on political issues as they fight for a spot in Congress - The New Hampshire
content: DURHAM- On Oct. 5, the University of New Hampshire (UNH) hosted the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum in the Memorial Union Building. Republican nominee Anthony DiLorenzo and Democratic nominee Stefany Shaheen were both given 35 minutes to share their opinions on what issues in New Hampshire are important to them and what their goals are if they were to win the election on November third. Stefany Shaheen at the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum The conversation was hosted by the Carsey School of Public Policy. The Forum is a nonpartisan series for congressional nominees in New Hampshire. The conversation was moderated by Kevin Sullivan, UNH Alum and a Washington Post Pulitzer Prize Winner. One of Shaheen's main topics was ending the war in Iran: “We're now seeing $4 gas prices; this wasn't a reality till this war started.” Shaheen says that she has heard from at least one person every day in the last two weeks worrying about gas prices this winter. Shaheen wants to see this war come to an end, and points out the soldiers that have been lost through its duration. “We've got to bring an end to this war, and Congress can do it,” Shaheen says. DiLorenzo comments on the fact that “we can not be the world's police officers.”  He says he is not “for boots on the ground” in this war and doesn't support the fact that the Iranian government should have nuclear weapons. DiLorenzo finds it strange that an oil-producing country would need to produce nuclear energy, but he says that foreign policy is not at the top of his priority list. Anthony DiLorenzo at the Carsey Candidate Policy Forum When the topic of artificial intelligence was brought up, Shaheen expressed concerns. “We should be focused on innovation that lifts everyone up, not wipes everyone out,” Shaheen says. She urges Washington to put up guardrails. DiLorenzo points out that there is good and bad in all technology. While it can be scary and unknown, he trusts the experts when they say it's containable. He does agree with his opponent that there needs to be guardrails added “to ensure privacy is protected.” Throughout the debate, Shaheen comments on DiLorenzo's support of President Donald Trump. Trump has endorsed DiLorenzo for the Congressional District race. On social media, Trump calls DiLorenzo a “very successful Businessman and Entrepreneur,” which is a point DiLorenzo uses during his campaign. “We need more business people in D.C.,” DiLorenzo says. He points out that he has worked since he was 8 years old and calls his opponent privileged due to their family. Shaheen then comments on how ICE has affected the state of New Hampshire. “This is not helping our community be safer,” Shaheen says. She mentions that the Department of Homeland Security shared that only 5% of people who are being detained have been charged with violent crimes. Shaheen speaks on hearing personal stories from families affected by ICE. DiLorenzo comments that we need immigration reform and that policies should reflect what the country needs. He believes that there is room for improvement; law enforcement needs more training and proper training. Both candidates agree that there is a housing issue in the Granite State. DiLorenzo comments on the high cost of infrastructure, but is still in favor of building. He comments on the fact that housing prices are outpacing wages. Shaheen makes a point of the tariffs' effect on our country. “Tariffs have wreaked havoc,” Shaheen says. She makes a statement claiming DiLorenzo’s support of these tariffs. She believes that they are hurting small businesses. Each candidate was given a minute to close. Shaheen declares that she is going to work hard for change in this country, and for its people’s support. “We have a choice between change or more of the same,” Shaheen says. She again highlights her opponent's support for the tariffs, war, and Trump. Shaheen speaks directly to UNH students, telling them to vote. “Don't let anyone tell you you're not allowed to vote.” DiLorenzo considers the election to be a “simple choice.” He calls Shaheen a “political insider who has come from a fairly privileged family,” and points out that the experience he brings is hard work and business. “We need more common sense business leadership in D.C. and less professional politicians, and that's why I'm running,” DiLorenzo says. With the election coming up, many are wondering what's next and who will win at the polls.

title: The Learning Landscape: The New England Agroforester - Fall Equinox 2026 - University of New Hampshire
content: ADAPT’s second Agroforestry Educator Cohort launched this July with a two-day immersive learning experience, gathering 13 educators from Vermont, New Hampshire, and Massachusetts. Beginning at Dartmouth College, Professor Theresa Ong and graduate student Krystal Bagnaschi introduced participants to key agroforestry concepts and shared the goals and vision of the ADAPT program. The group then toured several research and demonstration sites, including two food forests, the Experimental Linear Gap (ELG) research area, where a variety of forest farming crops are being studied, and an edible riparian buffer designed to support both ecological and food production goals. The riparian buffer was established in partnership with ReTreeUS, and Executive Director Richard Hodges joined the group to discuss food forest design and the organization's growing network of high school food forests throughout New England. On the second day, participants visited the Abenaki Garden in Hartford, Vermont, where Earl Hatley shared the story of the Community and Culture Acre, a teaching garden that also produces food and seeds for local food banks. Alongside the traditional Three Sisters planting, the site features hazelnuts, elderberries, ground cherries, and blueberries, with ongoing efforts to expand the area into a mature food forest system. The cohort concluded its field experience at Howling Wolf Farm in Randolph, Vermont, where Jenn Colby showcased her innovative approach to creating silvopasture through ecological succession. Participants learned how rotationally grazed sheep are integrated into the landscape, helping transform emerging woodlands into productive agroforestry systems while supporting animal welfare and ecosystem health. Looking ahead, both Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 participants will continue their field-based learning in Year 2 of the program. Upcoming visits include The Ecology School in Saco, Maine, on October 5 and the New Hampshire State Forest Nursery in Boscawen, NH, on November 13. For more information, contact State Coordinator Mike Smith at 4-H Community Agriculture and NH Ag in the Classroom. Two educators from the UNH Extension agroforestry program were recently featured on the Northeast Farm to School Collaborative's podcast, The Farm to School Podcast. Becky Denslow, a participant in the second Maple Tales cohort and now a member of the second ADAPT Agroforestry cohort, joined Mary Hartigan Demers, a member of the first ADAPT Agroforestry cohort, to share their experiences bringing agroforestry and maple education into their schools. The conversation highlights how educators are creating meaningful connections between students, trees, food systems, and local landscapes. Mary discusses developing a maple sugaring program at her middle school in downtown Manchester, and Becky reflects on her continuing agroforestry journey through multiple UNH Extension programs. An upcoming episode will feature Megan Glenn and other program leaders discussing the ADAPT Agroforestry program and cohorts, helping share lessons and successes from educators across the region. Listen to the episode on the Northeast Farm to School Collaborative's podcast page: The Farm to School Podcast. Members of the ADAPT Team participated in Erik Schellenberg's Temperate Syntropic Agroforestry webinar in August 2026. Drawing on his experience developing syntropic agroforestry systems in southern New York, Erik shared practical lessons, observations, and reflections from the field. Resources from the presentation include: Building on the introductory session, a second webinar on December 3, 2026 will take a deeper look at the theory, principles, and ecological relationships that underpin syntropic agroforestry. While some foundational concepts will be revisited, the session will be valuable for both those returning and those new to the approach. Participants are encouraged to bring questions about adapting syntropic practices to temperate climates. For more information, contact Jonathan Bates at Cornell Cooperative Extension. ReTreeUS Founder and Program Manager Richard Hodges prepares to plant a tree at a school site. Image credit: ReTreeUS. Discussions at the recent ADAPT all-hands meeting emphasized a challenge familiar to many agroforestry practitioners: how to establish educational plantings that remain productive, relevant, and well-maintained over time. ReTreeUS, a nonprofit organization working throughout New England, has spent the past 15 years developing and refining systems designed specifically to address those challenges in school settings. Founded by Richard Hodges, ReTreeUS began with a focus on helping schools create outdoor learning spaces centered around orchards and gardens. Over time, the organization found that long-term success depended not only on planting trees and gardens but also on developing practical approaches to maintenance, educator engagement, and curriculum integration. To date, ReTreeUS has helped establish more than 120 school and community orchards across Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, and Massachusetts. The organization originally set a goal of creating 100 school community orchards and has since expanded its focus to include school food forests. Over the next three years, the organization plans to establish 30 school food forests, including seven new sites this year. Foresters, farmers, technical advisors, service partners, and researchers observing tree plantings at a forest farming site at the ADAPT Project’s Fall 2026 All-Hands meeting. The ReTreeUS approach centers around systems that fit the realities of school operations. School gardens often face challenges related to summer maintenance, staff turnover, and weed management. To address these, ReTreeUS developed a "back-to-school garden" model. Schools receive trays of established crops such as lettuce and kale sourced from nearby farms. Students plant the seedlings in September, allowing gardens to become immediately productive while reducing summer maintenance demands. Cover crops help suppress weeds, improve soil health, and support pollinators during periods when students are not present. The organization's orchard model similarly prioritizes long-term stewardship. Typical school orchard plantings include 12 to 20 semi-dwarf fruit trees, often apples, pears, and peaches. ReTreeUS has developed deer-management strategies, planting protocols, and maintenance resources that schools can implement after installation. Teacher caretakers may receive stipends for ongoing stewardship, accompanied by progress reports and photographs documenting orchard development. Educational resources are another core component of the model. ReTreeUS provides standards-aligned lessons, presentations, videos, and enrichment materials that help teachers use orchards and food forests as living classrooms. By connecting outdoor spaces directly to existing curricula, orchards become more fully integrated into school operations and student learning. The organization's current food forest initiative expands on lessons learned through its orchard program. While each site is adapted to local conditions, plantings typically include multiple layers of perennial food-producing species. Fruit and nut trees may be combined with blueberries, raspberries, strawberries, grapevines, hazelnuts, perennial herbs, native plums, bush cherries, Cornelian cherries, and nitrogen-fixing species such as gomi. Clover is commonly seeded throughout the site as a living groundcover that suppresses weeds and contributes nitrogen to the system. One challenge ReTreeUS has worked to address is the perception that food forests are difficult to manage or appear untidy. School sites often require landscapes that are both ecologically functional and visually organized. Sheet mulching, straw, paper, defined planting zones, and groundcover establishment reduce competition from weeds while maintaining an appearance appropriate for educational campuses. Many of these plantings begin producing harvestable crops within the first year, particularly berries, herbs, and other perennial species. This early productivity helps sustain student interest while providing opportunities to explore topics such as food production, ecology, pollination, soil health, and agroforestry. Feedback from participating schools consistently highlights student engagement. Educators report that outdoor learning environments often create opportunities for students who may struggle in traditional classroom settings to participate in different ways. Planting, observing, harvesting, and caring for perennial systems allows students to engage directly with ecological processes over multiple seasons. For ADAPT partners exploring agroforestry in educational settings, the ReTreeUS model offers a practical example of how long-term stewardship, curriculum integration, and maintenance planning can support the success of school-based agroforestry projects. As interest in school food forests continues to grow across New England, these experiences provide useful insights into how agroforestry systems can become lasting educational and community assets. title: SHARPP hosts annual 'Take Back the Night' event - The New Hampshire
content: On the night of Thursday Oct. 15, on the Thompson Hall lawn at the University of New Hampshire, the SHARPP Center for Interpersonal Violence Awareness, Prevention, and Advocacy hosted its annual Take Back the Night (TBTN) event, an event that has been hosted since 1981. TBTN is an awareness event for victims of interpersonal violence. The event calls people to action and holds a vigil. While some attendees were wrapping chilled hands around warm cups of apple cider, tea, or hot chocolate provided by UNH catering, others were busy creating posters with encouraging messages reminding people they are never alone. “This event is important, it’s showing campus how interpersonal violence affects campus, and it gives survivors a place to speak and be heard where they otherwise aren't able to be,” said Rachel Stewart, the director of SHARPP. As the event opened, every attendee was given a glowstick which was later used in an activity to show how every person at the event had been impacted by interpersonal violence, either directly or indirectly. UNH Acapella group, The New Hampshire Notables have performed at the past three TBTN events. This year they chose to perform the song “Can't Catch Me Now” by Olivia Rodrigo, to highlight the struggle and resilience of interpersonal violence survivors. Their contribution was a moment of calm to help attendees transition into the open mic segment of the event. At the start of the open mic, Stewart briefly mentioned recent events at Cornell University involving interpersonal violence, highlighting its ubiquitous nature on college campuses. The event then moved into the speaker portion of the open mic. “I want people to know that this community is for them,” said Darian Kavlahao, one of the event MCs for TBTN. Many attendees got the opportunity to either speak or listen to the stories of others, sharing awareness and creating a supportive and inclusive environment. “[Interpersonal violence] is a part of my story, but it is not the whole story.” said Emma Schmidl-Gagne, a community advisor for SHARPP and the other event MC. While many were sharing their stories, each attendee was also given a candle that was lit and held for the remainder of the event. As the event ended with many feeling less alone, Stewart reminds all that this does not end here. “This event is great, but it can't just be one night. Everyone needs to care about interpersonal violence, it has to be every day,” Stewart said. SHARPP Center resources are available for all. The SHARPP Center is located on the 3rd Floor of Smith Hall. Resources include scheduling a meeting or contacting the SHARPP office at (603) 862- 3494. SHARPP also has a 24/7 helpline at (603) 862-7233. Drop-in hours have been temporarily paused for Fall 2026 due to staffing constraints. However, you can still stop by or contact SHARPP to make a virtual or in-person appointment. The SHARPP Center offers confidential appointments and a safe space to meet with staff and representatives.

title: Learning Curve - University of New Hampshire
content: These experiences, and many more, await the undergraduates who venture beyond the classroom to conduct their own research. They learn by doing, gain access to sophisticated tools, and forge distinctive relationships with faculty mentors. The work can be surprising, disgusting, challenging — but it’s always enlightening and, for most, transformative. UNH, as a public research institution with a roll-up-our-sleeves, git ’er done ethic that drives innovation and problem-solving, stokes the curiosity of these nascent explorers with opportunities galore. This exceptional commitment to undergraduate research results in nearly 2,000 students presenting at the annual Undergraduate Research Conference, one of the nation’s largest. Read on to meet some student researchers funded by the Hamel Center for Undergraduate Research, whose passion for discovery is leading them to real-world skills — and solutions. Mentor: Nathan Furey, associate professor of biological sciences Research: Identification of River Herring Predators in the Bellamy River “I started looking for opportunities during my freshman year and have been working with Dr. Furey ever since. My experience conducting undergraduate research has been full of cool discoveries, interesting challenges, and lots of time out in the field. [I remember] sitting on a little island in the middle of the Bellamy River on my first photo download day, nervous about not seeing anything on the cameras, and immediately opening to a photo of a great blue heron with a river herring in its beak. This was exactly what we were hoping to find!” Mentor: Otto Luna, digital resources curator, art and art history “I have been able to do archival research on art pieces as well as dive deeply into art provenance and how it impacts cultural heritage. As I’m looking toward the future, I hope to use my research skills and knowledge gained during this experience to break into the small field of art conservation in public art institutions. Being able to do under-graduate research also prepares me for master’s programs and better fills out my undergraduate resume of skills.” Mentor: Dante Scala, professor of political science and international affairs Research: Intraparty Ideological Conflict: A Case Study of the 2026 NH-01 Primary Elections “I am conducting interviews with candidates, visiting campaign events, studying political science literature, and conducting textual analyses of candidates’ policy statements. It has been an incredible privilege to be able to meet candidates in person and speak to them directly. This has been the best and most unique part of the project. It adds a human element to the other more technical and theoretical aspects of the project.” Program of study: marine, estuarine, and freshwater biology and sustainability Mentor: Nathan Furey, associate professor of biological sciences Research: Investigating Diets of Striped Bass and Atlantic Cod and the Energy Content of Their Prey “This experience has been much more broad than I was expecting because our lab is so collaborative. My favorite part of this experience was working with New Hampshire Fish and Game on its bag seine survey to collect fish samples for the prey energy density portion of my study. I enjoyed cruising around the bay, wading through varying levels of muddy substrate, and the excitement of seeing what cool fish we caught in the net. All of these hands-on experiences will definitely help me succeed in the future as I am now familiar with many different fisheries-related techniques.” Program of study: music performance; neuroscience and behavior Mentors: David Upham, associate professor of music education, and Kate Christison-Lagay, assistant professor of biological sciences Research: Emotional Responsiveness to Western Classical Music in Musicians versus Non-Musicians (with Tara Saran '27 and Nicole Di Benedetto '27) “A standout moment was when we first unboxed our pupillometer (the device for measuring pupil size) in my professor's lab. The whole team was there, and it was super exciting to see the device we had been discussing for months actually in the lab. It was also really exciting when we had our first participant in the lab and saw our program being used and heard their thoughts on the music after all of the work that built up to it.” Mentor: Casey Roark, assistant professor of psychology Research: Categorization Comparing Gamified and Traditional Conditions Provided Physically or Digitally “I have always loved asking questions about the world around me. This experience gave me a look into what being a researcher means and how to problem-solve when conducting my own study.” Mentors: Sajay Arthanat, professor of occupational therapy, and Marguerite Corvini, clinical assistant professor and director of simulation and digital health Research: An Innovative Virtual Reality-Based Peer Wellness Program for Rural Care Providers I have gained both technical knowledge and experience through my research, but most importantly I have seen how research affects people firsthand. Even before I had the true, numerical results, I could see how what I was doing was changing lives.” Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: UnitedHealth Stock Forecast: UNH Tests $421.87 Fibonacci Resistance as Post-Earnings Rally Extends - FXLeaders
content: Quick Answer: As of Tuesday, October 20, UnitedHealth Group (UNH) was trading at approximately $421.50, up around 3.5% on the day and extending a rebound from the $362.74 October low. The rebound is a continuation of a move stemming from the company’s Q3 results, which it said reflect “the discipline and execution” of its teams. The company also raised its full-year guidance for the third time this year, taking the 2026 adjusted EPS floor to $20.50. On the daily chart, the stock has broken a descending trendline from the July highs and is currently pressing the 61.8% Fibonacci level at $421.87. My view: UNH is bullish as long as it trades above $399.37. A break above $421.87 would likely lead to a target of $440.19 and $458.51. UNH was up around 3.51% on Tuesday, more than double the 1.54% move in the healthcare services and equipment sector. No news was reported to have caused the move. This puts Tuesday’s rally as an extension of the move the stock started on Wednesday, October 14, the day after the company reported Q3 results. For the quarter, UnitedHealth Group reported an adjusted EPS of $4.69, topping the $4.14 consensus, and the company cited “disciplined execution”. As a result, the company raised its full-year guidance to a minimum of $20.50, from its prior range of $19.50 to $20.00. Revenue during the quarter fell to $112.7 billion from $113.2 billion in the same quarter last year. However, earnings from operations improved to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion, the medical care ratio improved to 88.4% from 89.9% and UnitedHealthcare’s operating margin improved to 3.3% from 2.1%. The company has purposely shed members. At the end of the quarter, UnitedHealthcare had 48.3 million members, down from 50.1 million a year earlier, and the company lost 935,000 members in its Medicare Advantage plans since year-end 2025. I would say the quality of the margin is the more interesting question. The current quarter had $610 million of favorable prior-period reserve development. Management also said commercial cost trends are running above its initial 11% assumption, and its 2027 pricing is based on the assumption those costs would continue. In the quarter, Optum Health lost 10% of its revenue to $22.9 billion, largely due to the loss of value-based care patients. But it was still able to improve its operating earnings to $735 million, compared to $41 million last year. Optum’s other units also improved. OptumInsight improved earnings to $1.3 billion from $920 million and Optum Rx improved earnings to $1.7 billion from $1.5 billion. Optum Rx now has more than 50 percent of its membership from external clients, further reducing its reliance on UnitedHealthcare members. Operating cash flow of $5.1 billion, or 1.2 times net income, funded share repurchases and the $9.28 annual dividend. According to CFO Wayne DeVeydt on the latest earnings call, analyst consensus for 2027 “may understate the opportunity ahead.” DeVeydt added that a starting point for 2027 might be the low end of the company’s 13% to 16% long-term growth target, which is 13%. With 13% growth on the current $20.50 floor, we would see EPS at $23.17 in 2027, per calculations by Stocktwits. Management has said they will provide a more robust 2027 outlook by year-end. Risks for 2027 are mainly with the company’s Medicare Advantage (MA) business. About 69% of members in 2027 are in 4-Star or greater plans; a reduction from the current year. Plus, about 390,000 members are in MA plans that will not be offered in 2027. Also, two Medicare Advantage investigations by the DOJ remain open. UNH’s stock price, about $421.50, puts it at 20.6 times the 2026 EPS floor and 18.2 times the implied 2027 EPS. Post-earnings targets cluster around these numbers. Baird cut its target to $427, Barclays to $440, and Raymond James to $450, per Benzinga. More bullish targets include $504 from Piper Sandler and $500 from Bernstein, which cut from $512. The stock trades just under the lower targets, and with the latest Q3 beat, and an anticipated 2027 outlook by year-end, I think the upside is greater than the 2027 outlook. UnitedHealth is currently trading at $421.50, a 3.5% gain on the day, and is extending a sharp rebound after dropping to $362.74 in October, which was close to the 200 day EMA. The stock has not only cleared the 50 day EMA at $388.37, but also a descending trend line from the July peak, making the near term trend bullish. One thing worth noting is that price has reached the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level at $421.87, which is often a make-or-break level and in this case could indicate where the recent recovery stops. The 14 day relative strength index (RSI) has hit an overbought level at 72.10, the first time this has happened since May. Similar to the above reasoning, I view this as a caution flag. Above current resistance at $421.87, the next resistance levels are $440.19, which is the Barclays price target, and then the July high at $458.51. The current level of support at $410.51 is also the 50% Fibonacci retracement level. Below that is support at $399.37, which is the 38.2% Fibonacci retracement level, and below that the key level at $388.37 to $385.23, which is where the 50 day EMA meets the 23.6% Fibonacci retracement, and below that is the 200 day EMA and the October low at $362.74. I am bullish as long as UnitedHealth remains above $399.37. A break below that level would put focus on $388.37 and $385.23 and a close below the 50 day EMA would also be bearish. UnitedHealth Group (UNH) extended its post-earnings rally on Tuesday after reporting Q3 results and raising its 2026 guidance for the third time. UNH stock gained about 3.5% on the day, more than double the gain of the healthcare services sector. The key level is the 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level at $421.87. A daily close above that level opens up $440.19 and the July high at $458.51. Management has stated they would issue a fuller 2027 outlook by year-end. They have not specified a date, but results for Q4 are expected to be released in late January 2027.

title: Visiting UNH? Five reasons to also tour UNH's College of Life Sciences and Agriculture - University of New Hampshire
content: If you're interested in life sciences, agriculture, environmental science, nutrition, genetics, marine biology, or any of the programs in UNH’s College of Life Sciences and Agriculture, a dedicated COLSA academic tour gives you a closer look at the college, the people, and the opportunities that would shape your four years here. Here are five reasons it's worth adding a COLSA tour to your campus visit and admissions general tour.Register for a UNH COLSA academic tour 1. You'll see the spaces where COLSA students work, do research, and learn The UNH general admissions tour shows you residence halls, dining, and the main campus. A COLSA academic tour takes you into the college’s classrooms, teaching and research labs, and research facilities. COLSA students work across a range of hands-on environments like research labs, greenhouses, animal facilities, and field sites connected to New Hampshire's forests, farms, and coastline. Seeing some of those spaces in person helps you understand what "hands-on learning" looks like in your field of interest, before you commit. 2. You can ask questions that are specific to your COLSA major interests A COLSA academic tour is designed specifically for students interested in the college's programs and majors. Current COLSA students lead the tour, and faculty get involved, too. Every tour includes a Q&A session with a faculty member where you can ask questions about specific majors, research opportunities, and what life looks like as a COLSA student. If you're trying to decide between majors, like wildlife and conservation biology and environmental conservation and sustainability, or between the nutrition dietetics option and the health and wellness option, this is the right place to ask. 3. You'll get a clearer picture of where a degree from UNH’s College of Life Sciences and Agriculture can take you One of the most common questions prospective students and families have is: “What can I actually do with this degree?” COLSA's outcomes data offers a starting point. The most recent First Destination Survey shows 93% of COLSA grads are employed or in graduate school. During the tour, you’ll hear directly from current students and faculty about how those outcomes connect to specific programs, internships, and research experiences. Alumni have been in roles like Public Program Educator at the Audubon Society of Rhode Island and Community Outreach Manager for the Seacoast Science Center Marine Mammal Rescue Program. A COLSA visit gives you the chance to ask how students get from the classroom to careers like those. 4. A COLSA tour can help you figure out your major, even if you're undecided You don't need to have your major figured out before you visit. In fact, many UNH first-year students arrive on campus undeclared or change their major at least once before graduating. A COLSA academic session can help you start narrowing things down. That's a wide range of fields, so visiting COLSA, hearing how faculty and students describe the work, and seeing labs in person can help you identify which direction feels right, or rule out options that don't. If you're still exploring after you’re a Wildcat, COLSA's St. Martin Career Exploration Office is a resource for students working through those questions once they're enrolled. 5. Why visiting UNH’s College of Life Sciences and Agriculture before you apply is worth your time Visiting before you apply or before you commit is one of the most practical things you can do to make this important decision with more confidence. A COLSA academic tour is an opportunity to see the college as it is, ask more in depth questions, and get a feel for whether this is the right environment for you. If you're already planning to visit UNH, adding a COLSA academic session to your itinerary can give you significantly more information to work with when making your college decisions. title: Occupational Therapy Conference Returns to UNH for Third Year - University of New Hampshire
content: UNH will welcome occupational therapy professionals and students from across the state and region on Nov. 14 for the New Hampshire Occupational Therapy Association (NHOTA) Fall Conference. It marks the third consecutive year UNH has hosted the annual conference, which has grown significantly in recent years. Organizers expect between 150 and 200 attendees this fall, compared with roughly 30 to 40 participants when the conference was smaller. The conference brings together occupational therapists for a day of continuing education and professional collaboration, including a keynote presentation, breakout sessions and scholarly poster presentations. For UNH, it also provides an opportunity to bring professionals to campus while showcasing the work of occupational therapy students and faculty. "We love hosting the conference. In a way, it feels like welcoming guests into our home,” says Casey Rabideau, clinical assistant professor of occupational therapy and UNH's liaison to NHOTA. “It is an opportunity to bring visibility to our program, build alumni relationships, and showcase our work at many different levels." UNH students will have an active presence at the conference, presenting research from honors projects, master's theses, and doctoral capstones, while faculty will also lead conference sessions. This year's presentations highlight the range of work happening at UNH. Rabideau will join students and Sarah Valli from the UNH Institute on Disability for a session on improving access to assistive technology. Their work includes an initiative in which students use 3D printing to create assistive devices for people with disabilities across New Hampshire. Other presentations will explore socially assistive robots for Alzheimer's and dementia home care, artificial intelligence's potential role in occupational therapy, and how occupational therapy fieldwork and doctoral capstone students can support school systems. Beyond the presentations, Rabideau says the conference gives students a chance to network directly with professionals in the field. "Our state is small, so having close to 175 practitioners come together is quite significant," Rabideau says. "For our students, that one-on-one interaction is important. They might meet someone from a future fieldwork site or hear about a job opening. It creates opportunities to network and start thinking about career pathways." The conference will also feature a keynote panel from the Krempels Center, where individuals will share their lived experiences with disability and occupational therapy, helping practitioners reconnect with the impact and purpose of their work. Hosting the conference comes at a time of growth for UNH's occupational therapy program. The program recently celebrated its 80th anniversary, and Rabideau says student numbers are increasing. UNH has also expanded its occupational therapy pathways with the addition of the occupational therapy doctorate (OTD), which recently graduated its first class. Rabideau says consistently bringing professionals to UNH strengthens connections between the university and the state's occupational therapy community while also giving students a glimpse of where their education can take them. "It's a reminder of their next step for them, too," Rabideau says. "It's like, 'Oh, this is the next real thing for me,' which can be really fun." Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: Honorary Degree Surprise for 101st Birthday Brings Wildcats From Two Generations Together - University of New Hampshire
content: Dan Carr ’85 and Dr. Julian Silverblatt at Silverblatt's 101st birthday celebration. When you have as much time for comparison under your belt as Dr. Julian Silverblatt does, certain proclamations can carry a little more weight. Silverblatt recently declared his 101st birthday – celebrated this summer in his hometown of Houston, Texas – his best one yet. Given the catalog of calendar flips he had to choose from, such a stance felt particularly momentous. Then again, given the circumstances, it also didn’t seem all that far-fetched. It’s not every day that you turn 101 years old in a room full of friends and family wearing a borrowed cap and gown while receiving an honorary degree from a beloved institution, a degree presented by someone who went from perfect stranger to future family Christmas card recipient in a matter of hours. Silverblatt was surprised on his 101st birthday with an honorary degree from UNH, a special delivery cooked up by his daughters to honor their father’s cherished time as a student while he was in the military. Circumstances of his arrangement ultimately prevented him from graduating, but he always looked back on his Durham days fondly. The family wanted the degree presented by someone with UNH connections, and that person wound up being Dan Carr ’85, a fellow Houston resident who had never even heard of the Silverblatt family when Julian’s daughters cold-called him at work one afternoon to make a pitch for his assistance. Carr was happy to oblige, the honorary degree was presented, and by the end of the celebration, Silverblatt was the proud owner of both a treasured UNH memento and a meaningful friendship forged with a fellow Wildcat more than 40 years his junior. “He said, ‘This is the best birthday I’ve ever had.’ It really meant a lot to him,” Terri Brown, the oldest of Julian’s three daughters, says. “He was totally surprised. Someone asked me if he cried, and he’s not a crier, but the smile on his face said it all.” It was a whirlwind experience for all involved. The family had to pass on UNH’s invitation for Silverblatt to attend commencement to receive the degree – even though her father “walks faster than me, still drives and takes himself to get his haircut whenever he needs to,” Terri quips. In the end Silverblatt’s daughters – Terri and sisters Pamela and Cindy – wound up with less than a week to find a UNH representative who could be on hand for the celebration in Houston. And Carr, for his part, was working in his office on an otherwise normal Wednesday when he received a phone call from the office receptionist. “I got a call from reception and she said, ‘I’ve got three daughters on the line that want to talk to you.’ It was Cindy who spoke, and she said, ‘Are you Dan Carr? Are you a grad of UNH? Because I’ve got a really strange request to ask of you,’” Carr says. So how did the family come to choose Carr as the potential UNH representative? A quick Google search and an alphabetical list. It was Cindy who did the sleuthing, finding a guest list from a UNH alumni reception held at the Houston Space Center in 2020 (only days before the start of the COVID shutdown). She decided to start alphabetically at the top of the list and begin making cold calls. It only took one. Though Carr, the first name on the list, had never met a member of the family prior to the phone call, his involvement was a pretty easy sell. Beyond the endearingly quirky nature of the story, the situation prompted him to think of his own father, who at 96 years old had just entered home hospice care. “I’m really happy they reached out to me, because my dad had not been doing so well, so it feels really good to be able to help out another family who wanted to come together for their father,” says Carr. For the celebration, Terri and her sisters secured a cap and gown from Silverblatt’s daughter-in-law, Shelley Silverblatt, asked their father to don it, and had Carr surprise him with the honorary degree. But that was only the beginning of the connection. The pair spent the rest of the brunch becoming fast friends. “What’s really cool is that the thing we had in common is that we walked the same campus about 40 years apart,” Carr says. “It was really neat to share stories with him and his family about that, to learn about his experience at UNH and beyond. His daughters said, ‘Dan, please give us your address because we want to make sure you are part of our Christmas card circulation.’” “He could have been a long-lost member of the family. It was just incredible to pick a stranger out of the clear blue sky and have him be so personable and just fit so seamlessly with our family,” says Terri. “That to me was overwhelming, just how wonderful Dan was. I can’t sing his praises enough. He just made the day that much more special.” Silverblatt’s UNH story is a unique one very much of his time. Originally from Cincinnati, Ohio, Silverblatt was assigned to UNH through the Army Specialized Training Program (ASTP) during World War II. The program, created in 1942, identified academically talented enlisted men and sent them to college campuses for accelerated training in engineering, foreign languages, medicine, and other specialized technical fields. Silverblatt completed pre-medical coursework at UNH from 1943 to 1944. Although he didn’t graduate, his academic work at UNH was a key piece in enabling him to enroll in medical school without first earning an undergraduate degree. Silverblatt went on to earn his medical degree from the University of Cincinnati and served for more than 50 years as a practicing physician in the Houston area. “He was taking almost exclusively science classes” at UNH, Terri says, and before he left, he had “completed all the science requirements for going to medical school, so the Army just sent him on to medical school at the University of Cincinnati. He was 19 years old when he started there and didn’t have a bachelor’s degree.” Carr arrived on UNH’s campus about four decades later, and met his wife, Kari Kaalstad, while they were both students (the couple celebrated their 37th wedding anniversary in June). He looks back fondly on his days as a student and member of the rowing team at UNH and also participated for three years in helping to lead orientation for first-year students. “I have some friends for life from those years, that’s for sure,” Carr says. He may have made another in Silverblatt. The two talked about a lot more than just their individual times as UNH students, connecting over each other’s family histories and baseball rooting interests (Carr’s father grew up rooting for the New York/San Francisco Giants, and Silverblatt supported the Cincinnati Reds). They also talked hobbies, and although some of those overlap a little less, a future reconnection could still be in the cards. “It was just really fun to connect with him. I’d love to see him again – even though I don’t play bridge,” Carr quips. “It was really fun, and it’s amazing that it was UNH that brought us together.” Given all of the logistics involved, the celebration couldn’t have come together any better. Silverblatt’s daughters were able to honor their father and commemorate an important time in his life while also creating an unexpected connection across UNH generations. Silverblatt and Carr had distinctly different experiences at UNH, but both have reason to draw on lasting memories as students that impacted them for decades beyond their time on campus. And the birthday celebration put them in the same room to do so together. Which begs the question, what exactly does Silverblatt’s family have planned for an encore? “I am all about doing whatever I can to make him happy, and it’s funny because people have asked me, ‘what are you going to do next year?’ I honestly don’t know, but it’s going to take me a little while to think of something that could top this one,” Terri says. title: What Makes a Walk in the Woods Good for Your Mental Health? UNH Research Offers New Clues - University of New Hampshire
content: UNH researchers studied visitors to College Woods to better understand how perceptions of biodiversity and natural sounds relate to mental well-being. Ever wonder why a walk through College Woods after spending hours studying can do wonders for your mood? While past research has shown that spending time outdoors can improve mental well-being, new UNH research offers a closer look at what makes those experiences so beneficial. In a yearlong study at College Woods, researchers found that visitors' perceptions of biodiversity — the many species living in the woods — and the sounds they experienced were closely linked to mental well-being. They also found that something as simple as an educational sign highlighting biodiversity could give visitors' moods an additional boost. The study, published in Landscape and Urban Planning, was led by an interdisciplinary team that included Lauren Ferguson, assistant professor of recreation management and policy, Remington Moll, associate professor of natural resources and the environment, Laura Kloepper, associate professor of biological sciences, UNH graduate student Anna Frisbie, and Karina Sanchez, assistant professor of biology from California State University, Dominguez Hills. “Previous nature-health research had a major limitation: it could tell us that ‘biodiversity is good for mental health’ but couldn't tell land managers, park planners, or healthcare providers what to actually do with that information,” Ferguson says. “The research lacked specificity about which aspects of biodiversity matter most and how to enhance the mental health benefits of nature visits.” Between June 2023 and May 2024, researchers surveyed visitors to College Woods, a 230-acre natural area bordering the UNH campus, collecting 641 matched surveys before and after their visits. They also measured biodiversity using wildlife cameras, bird surveys, and vegetation records. Visitors reported more positive emotions, fewer negative emotions, and greater feelings of restoration, including relaxation and recovery from mental fatigue, after spending time in the woods. On average, participants' self-reported restoration scores increased by nearly 30% following their visits. Additionally, researchers found that visitors' overall perceptions of biodiversity were stronger predictors of mental well-being than the actual number of bird and mammal species researchers measured. The pleasantness of the sounds visitors experienced, such as birdsong, rustling leaves, and flowing water, was another strong predictor. The study also found that season influenced visitors' experiences. Participants reported greater feelings of restoration during spring and summer, but improvements in mood were observed regardless of season. “I was somewhat surprised by these findings; however, I've had similar results in another project,” Ferguson says. “I think that visitors to parks are more comfortable perceiving overall biodiversity and forest health and perhaps less comfortable identifying and counting specific species. This is something that we will continue to examine in future research.” To explore whether helping visitors recognize biodiversity could influence their experiences, the researchers placed an educational sign near the College Woods trail entrance during designated periods and removed it during others. The sign, titled "Meet the neighbors!" highlighted the forest's wildlife, including more than 20 mammal species, 50 bird species, and 110 plant and tree species. It encouraged visitors to look and listen for different species. Visitors who encountered the sign perceived slightly greater biodiversity than those who didn't. The sign was also positively associated with positive mood, although it did not show a meaningful relationship with reductions in negative emotions or increased restoration. “We think the signs may help people become more aware of the biodiversity around them and notice species they might otherwise miss,” Ferguson says. “That can create a stronger, more mindful connection with nature and turn a casual walk in the woods into a more restorative experience.” By shedding light on what makes time in nature beneficial, the findings offer insights for park managers, urban planners, and others responsible for maintaining public green space. “Our research shows that educational signs about biodiversity were linked to a boost in positive mood during forest visits,” Ferguson says. “Biodiversity education signs are a simple, inexpensive tool that forest managers can use to enhance those benefits.” For a university campus, where students often face academic pressures and mental-health challenges, the findings also underscore the potential value of accessible natural spaces such as College Woods, Ferguson adds. “I hope that people start to view small community forests like College Woods and other parks as more than just a space for recreation, but as critical health infrastructure,” Ferguson says. While the findings are specific to College Woods, where most participants were repeat visitors and many were connected to the university, Ferguson sees opportunities to build on the research. Future studies could explore whether similar results hold in other natural settings, incorporate physiological measures of well-being, and examine how different types of educational signage influence visitors' experiences.
